Communicating & Using Research

Communicating and using research — writing the report, presenting, referencing, and applying findings to practice.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Write a research report in the standard format
  • Present findings at conference and posters
  • Use correct referencing
  • Apply research findings to nursing practice

In simple words

Research that stays in a file is wasted. Reporting, presenting and applying findings complete the process.

Structure of a research report

Section Content
Title Short, clear and specific
Abstract Summary of the whole study
Introduction Background and need
Review of literature What is known and the gap
Methodology Design, sample, ethics, tools
Results Findings in tables and graphs
Discussion Meaning, comparison with literature, limitations
Conclusion and recommendations Implications and suggestions
References All sources cited
Appendices Tools and supplementary material

Referencing

  • Cite the source in the text and list it in the reference section
  • APA style: Author, initials (year), Title, Edition, Publisher
  • Vancouver: numbered citations in order of appearance
  • Consistent style, no missing reference and no unreferenced citation
  • Always avoid plagiarism

Using research in practice

  1. Ask a practice question (e.g. does hourly repositioning prevent pressure ulcers?)
  2. Acquire evidence from research and guidelines
  3. Appraise the quality and feasibility
  4. Apply to the ward with evaluation
  5. Assess the audit result and revise

🔴 A research report is a clinical tool

A well-written report tells the reader what was done, what was found and what should change. Present findings in plain words that colleagues in the ward can use.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Report sections: title, abstract, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion, references.
  2. Abstract summarises aim, methods, results and conclusion.
  3. APA and Vancouver are common referencing styles.
  4. Evidence-based practice follows ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess.
  5. Presentation and publication improve research utilisation.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Guidelines and protocols may be developed from research findings.
  2. Peer review improves the quality of research.
  3. Acknowledgements and declarations on conflicts of interest are needed.
  4. The discussion links findings to existing literature.
  5. Recommendations guide policy changes.

📌 Memory trick

Evidence steps: A-A-A-A-A — Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, Assess.

60-second revision

  • Report: title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion, references.
  • Present at conferences, in journals and posters.
  • Reference with APA or Vancouver; avoid plagiarism.
  • Utilise evidence: ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess.
  • Dissemination and application complete the research.

Test yourself

The section that summarises the whole study is:

Answer: B. The abstract summarises aim, methods, results and conclusion in a short paragraph.

Which style is commonly used for nursing references?

Answer: A. APA and Vancouver are standard academic referencing styles.

The first step in evidence-based practice is:

Answer: B. Evidence-based practice starts with asking a clear clinical question.

The purpose of the discussion section is to:

Answer: B. The discussion interprets the findings, compares with prior studies and states limitations.

Research utilisation means:

Answer: B. Utilisation is applying findings to change practice and improve patient outcomes.
